summary: 1 Maccabees 10 (89 verses) continues the story of faithfulness. Starting with 'In the one hundred sixtieth year, Alexander Epiphanes, the son of Antiochus, went up and took possession of Ptolemais. They received him, and he reigned there.', it moves through themes of faithfulness, wisdom and calls readers toward hope.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows faithfulness lived out in second temple period. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: In the one hundred sixtieth year, Alexander Epiphanes, the son of Antiochus, went up and took possession of Ptolemais. They received him, and he reigned there.
For the building of the walls of Jerusalem and fortifying it all around, the expense shall also be given out of the king’s revenue, also for the building of the walls in Judea.”
He sent him a gold buckle, as the custom is to give to the king’s kindred. He gave him Ekron and all its land for a possession.

questions.question: What is happening in 1 Maccabees 10?
questions.answer: In 89 verses, this chapter 1 maccabees 10 (89 verses) continues the story of faithfulness. starting with 'in the one hundred sixtieth year, alexander epiphanes, the son of antiochus, went up and took possession of ptolemais. they received him, and he reigned there.', it moves through themes of faithfulness, wisdom and calls readers toward hope. The setting is second temple period, written to jewish community. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote 1 Maccabees and why 10 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally anonymous / tradition, addressed to jewish community around intertestamental. This chapter fits the book's purpose as jewish literature — its themes of faithfulness, wisdom build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'covenant' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Binding promise/agreement God makes with people. In this chapter, it appears in context of faithfulness. For a first-time reader: think of it as binding promise/agreement god makes with people, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through faithfulness and wisdom, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 30 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'Instead of the third part of the seed, and instead of half of the fruit of the trees, which falls to me to receive, I release it from this day and henceforth, so that I will not ta...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about faithfulness. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
